### T-154 — The slow-step margin does not reach the registry's start steps

> _2026-09-26 · core/blong-gogo · open_

`log.slowMs` tunes the loader's steps and the retention store, and a runner may raise it for a
machine that is legitimately slow, but two callers of `withProgress` ignore it. `Registry.ts` passes
`getProgress` only for `create ports`, `start ports`, `ready ports` and `stop ports`, and
`core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/knex.ts`'s `ready` does the same for `schema table sync` and the
constraint pass, so all of them keep the compiled default of 1000ms and raising the margin cannot
silence them. If a slow startup ever warns under one of those labels, this is why. Give those calls
the configured margin — check first what the registry's `#config` carries, since the `log` block is
a platform-level sibling rather than part of the registry's section, while the knex adapter has the
same reach to `this.config`.

### T-183 — Log the gateway's effective port whether or not it was configured

> _2026-09-30 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Gateway.ts only speaks about the port when it was chosen at random, and only as a warn that is
suppressed at logLevel info and above: a statically configured port is never logged, and a random
one is silent in dev. Starting a gateway for the Storybook live modes therefore leaves an agent to
poll ss for a port it cannot be told about, and a server-only entry (gateway.port 0) gives no clue
either way. Emit the effective port once at startup — the configured value and the bound value — at
a level that survives the dev intent's log level.

### T-225 — A watch reply arrives empty across the request boundary

> _2026-10-05 · core/blong-gogo · open_

The cluster adapter watch verb answers {events: asyncGenerator, existing} and what reaches the
controller carries neither key: a probe logged no existing and no stream, on a watch that opened
successfully and repeated once a second at the pacing floor.

Now explained: the whole reply is dropped, not the stream within it, and only on the path that
crosses a transport — the deploy port's request call. A handler reaches the same adapter through the
in-process proxy and receives both the initial list and the generator intact (see T-227 for the
probe). That is why a watch opened correctly and delivered nothing: the adapter was fine, and the
values were gone before the controller saw them. The realm therefore runs its watch from a handler,
and the resync interval is no longer the only trigger that works.

### T-227 — The adapter replies null for a watch, and the generator dies there

> _2026-10-05 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Probed at the call site: cluster.custom.watch answers the packet
`[null, {mtid: response, method: cluster.custom.watch}]`, while cluster.custom.find answers real
data with the same coordinates, so the routing, the resource type and the group/version/plural are
all right and only the watch reply loses its value. The adapter carries no codec, so this is not a
wire encoding step, and it is not the meta wrapping either: what is left is the reply path around
the adapter handler.

Characterised on the second attempt. The loss is not in the adapter and not in the generator: a call
that reaches the adapter through a handler proxy carries the stream whole, and the realm's
kustomize.watch.run now logs "watch: open with 1 existing, stream present" and reconciles from the
list it receives. The call the port makes, through the deploy port's request path, is the one that
answers null. So the defect to fix is narrower than "a reply cannot carry a stream": a reply that
cannot be carried is replaced by a null instead of raising, and the caller cannot tell a dropped
result from an empty one. Fix the silence first (the reply path should refuse a value it cannot
carry), then decide whether the transport should carry the generator rather than only data.

### T-316 — Debug mode should answer what the ACL guard would run for a call

> _2026-10-10 · core/blong-gogo · open_

`aclCheckSql` is pure and exported, but reaching it with a real configuration meant a throwaway
script that rebuilt the resolved ACL config by hand, printed the SQL and substituted the bindings
one by one; that script has been dropped with the rest of the investigation. The question it
answered — what does the guard actually run for _this_ call — belongs to debug mode, beside
`/api/sys/config`, `/api/sys/methods` and `/api/sys/rpc`: an `/api/sys/acl` that takes a method and
a record (or a table and an entity) and returns the resolved configuration (the guarded table, the
scope predicates, the path types), the SQL and bindings `aclCheckSql` builds for it, and whether the
action is guarded at all — an unknown `actionId` short-circuits the whole expression to `TRUE`,
which is itself the answer to a surprising number of "why was this allowed" questions. The party
investigation needed it because the entire per-request ACL cost is one 4 KB boolean expression with
four correlated `EXISTS` sub-queries, and reading that out of the source is not the same as reading
it for the call being debugged. It stays behind `systemDebug`, which must never be enabled in
production, and it should be read-only: it reports the SQL, it never runs it against a caller's
record.

### T-321 — The shutdown bound and the pod grace are the same 30 seconds

> _2026-10-11 · core/blong-gogo · open_

runServer.ts bounds the graceful stop at timeoutMs ?? 30_000 and no call site passes one, while
neither the operator tree nor the suite tree writes terminationGracePeriodSeconds — the 30 the pods
carry is the Kubernetes default. The two bound the same interval from opposite ends, so if
platform.stop() ever hangs, blong's force-exit and the kubelet's SIGKILL land at the same instant:
SIGKILL can win, the pod dies 137 part-way through teardown, and the graceful shutdown timed out
marker that would have explained it is lost. Kubernetes' own guidance is that the application must
finish before the grace period does, which leaves two remedies with different owners — the internal
bound sits below the default (25s is the usual number) or the generator writes an explicit
terminationGracePeriodSeconds with a margin for every process it deploys. The signal path itself is
verified and needs nothing: the operator and a suite service each print the marker and exit 0 in the
same second the signal arrives, and the spawn test in this package proves it for the CLI through GNU
timeout.

### T-344 — A reload refuses a parent-declared key it would accept at startup

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · open_

The allow-list a module is validated against is captured when it loads, so the parent-declared half
of it is the parent's block as it was at startup. An rc edit that adds a key to a parent's block for
a child is therefore refused by that child's reload validator — with `unknown key` — even though the
same key is accepted at startup, so a legitimate new setting needs a restart.

To close it, thread the parent's block getter down alongside `blockOf`: the child already receives
its own candidate block by `blockOf(snapshot)`, and the parent could pass `Object.keys` of the
candidate's block for this child, computed from the same snapshot, so the check judges a reload with
the keys the reload actually declares. The keysOnEntry set needs the same treatment, or a group
config added by an edit stays refused.

### T-350 — Stop keying a realm child by its function name

> _2026-10-15 · core/blong-gogo · open_

A minification setting should not decide which realms exist. The loader in
`core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts` looks a child's config block up by the child function's name and skips
the child when there is no such key, so any build that drops function names loses realms silently —
this session lost the whole `ui` realm of a built Storybook that way (F-537). Ways out, roughly in
order of how much they change: make the loader load a child whose name is empty anyway (its own
`config.default` block applies, which for blong-browser is the same activation), accept
`{name, load}` objects as children so the key is declared rather than inferred from a function name,
or at least log a warning naming the child that was skipped instead of a debug line. Whichever is
chosen, the app build's `minify: false` and the Storybook build's should no longer be load-bearing.

### T-250 — An unreachable database can kill a process by event

> _2026-10-06 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Found while fixing an unrelated failure and not fixed with it. The knex adapter's start wraps
ensureDatabase in try/catch and warns, and the intent is plainly to continue: schema sync will
surface the real failure. What actually happened when the host did not resolve was a process-ending
error with a stack of one frame (getaddrinfo) and no await above it, which is the shape of an
unhandled error event on the mysql2 connection rather than a rejected promise the catch could see.
Confirm it by pointing a dev run at a name that does not resolve with the old code path, then make
the failure arrive through the caller: attach an error listener the moment the connection exists, or
let ensureDatabase reject in a way that does not also emit. It matters because a warn-and-continue
that kills the process is worse than a throw, which at least says where it came from.

### T-750 — An MLE message can be replayed; nothing in it says when

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · open_

MLE signs and encrypts a message but says nothing about _when_ it was made: the request is
JWS(payload) inside a JWE, the gateway `decryptVerify`s it and runs the handler, and there is no
`iat`, no `jti` or nonce, no sequence number and no cache of what was seen. A request body captured
whole therefore replays successfully for as long as its bearer token lives — and the bearer token is
the only thing bounding the window, because token replay itself is covered (sessions rotate the
refresh token, `docs/blong/docs/concepts/sessions.md`). Message replay is not.

It matters because MLE is the answer to an intermediary that can read bodies. That same intermediary
can resend them verbatim, so a call that is not idempotent by its own keys (a transfer, a role
grant) happens twice. Nothing in the protocol notices.

The fix is small and belongs in the protected header rather than the payload, so the AEAD tag covers
it: carry `iat` (clock) and a random `jti` in the JWE protected header beside `mlsk`/`mlek`; the
gateway refuses an `iat` outside a window and a `jti` it has already seen within it. The window's
memory is the part with a decision — an in-process bounded set is enough for one replica, while a
deployment with several needs a shared store (the `redis` adapter is already in these processes) or
a replay lands on another pod. Rollout needs a config gate rather than a surprise: a body without
`iat` is refused only once `mle.requireFreshness` is on, and the clients ship the header first.

Not to be confused with the stream work: a stream frame is a sequence, so its replay protection is
the frame counter (`@@D-948`), which is a different mechanism for a different shape.

### T-757 — Move the stub-generation pass out of schema(), after the load

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Move the generation pass out of `schema()` and into one sweep after the platform has loaded. Today
the pass pairs whatever exists when it runs: a definition is resolved as its layer loads and a group
folder is recorded when the watcher scans its realm, so a folder scanned after the definition is not
paired until the process restarts — the demo works because `orchestrator` sorts before `server`,
which is luck rather than a rule. A single sweep at the end of the load, or on `ready`, would remove
the ordering question and let the generator be tested without an API bundle being resolved first.
The dev gating that was part of this entry is done (D-963), and the scan reporting is done (D-961),
so what is left is the ordering alone. While there: the same folder is still scanned twice in one
load (two identical scan calls milliseconds apart), which is harmless now that nothing is reported
per scan but is a duplicate worth removing in the watcher.

### T-341 — Validate a config reload and reject an invalid snapshot

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · done_

The startup path validates every module's config block, but a hot reload is not validated:
ConfigRuntime.reload() builds the new snapshot, installs it and then notifies subscribers, so an rc
edit that introduces an unknown key is applied. The decision was to reject such a reload and keep
the previous snapshot. To finish: give ConfigRuntime a validator hook run before the snapshot is
installed, and collect one validator per module during the load. Each validator needs a getter that
re-derives its block from a candidate snapshot - capturing the parent's getter as a closure is the
natural way, which means threading the getter (or a path) through loadRealm's recursion; its call
sites are the loader's child calls and folderAnalysis' wrapper. Until then, document that only
startup is validated.

Done. ConfigRuntime gained setValidator, run before the installed snapshot: a rejected candidate
keeps the previous configuration, reports the rejection and yields an empty diff. The loader
collects one validator per module through a block getter threaded down the recursion, and the
watcher is attached at the end of the load because it did not exist where it was attached before.
Verified end to end with the watcher on. Design: D-548; the wiring defect found on the way: F-524.

database), because the two switches will otherwise be driven by different mechanisms and an operator
would have to know which is which.

### T-748 — A log tail could stream, if a subscription were a realm method

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · done_

Explored because the viewer page polls `viewer.entry.find` once a second (`@@D-946`). The
recommended shape is that a subscription is a method of a realm rather than a transport a realm
opens: `viewer.entry.stream` declared like any handler, granted by the same `viewerRead`, in the API
schema, mockable, traced as a flow, and implemented as an async generator that yields the backlog
from `after` and then each record as the adapter receives it. The transport stays the framework's,
selected by a route option beside the existing `rawBody`, `bundle` and `meter`, so the realm never
imports `ws`, never sees a socket and never checks a token.

SSE read through `fetch` is the recommended transport over WebSocket, and the deciding argument is
authentication rather than throughput: `new WebSocket()` and `EventSource` cannot send an
`Authorization` header, so a socket would need the token moved into a cookie or a query string — a
new auth surface, which is what `@@D-946` rejected — while a `fetch` plus `ReadableStream` read
sends the same bearer as every other call. SSE also needs nothing installed, needs no upgrade
handling at the ingress, and a log tail is one-way; `LogViewer` already filters client-side, so a
server-side filter is another request carrying `after`.

What the work would touch: `core/blong-gogo` for the route option, the frame writer, abort on close,
an overflow policy and the flow a subscription mints and ends; `core/blong-browser` for
`remote.stream(method, params)` returning an async iterator (deliberately not folded into
`handler[...]`, whose return type is one value); `tools/blong-log` for `subscribe?` beside `load` in
`LogViewerSource`; `realm/blong-viewer` for a listener set in the store and `viewerEntryStream`; and
one ingress annotation for nginx response buffering.

Two limits to carry into it: the buffer belongs to the one process that receives the records, so a
page served by another replica streams nothing until the store is shared or every replica receives a
copy; and a subscription is a long-lived flow, so it must be ended at disconnect and given a TTL so
a revoked capability takes effect on reconnect.

**Open question, asked in `#blong-ask` because the owner was away:** adopt the stream now over SSE,
adopt it over WebSocket instead, or record this design and keep polling. Nothing is implemented
until that answer arrives.

### T-756 — A quiet stream cannot be told from a dead one

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · done_

A subscription to a quiet process tells the reader nothing, and the portal's log page cannot tell
quiet from dead. The sealed binary envelope has no keep-alive: `writeEventStream` writes `: ping`
only for the text envelope, because "a binary reader has no comment frame to skip harmlessly"
(`@@F-808` context), and the frame format has no keepalive flag. The response headers ride with the
first frame, and through the dev proxy they do not reach the browser until the first body byte, so a
page that has just subscribed shows `data-stream="closed"` until something is written — up to the
15s text heartbeat, forever on the binary one. That is what leaves
`realm/blong-viewer/test/viewer.play.ts`'s "the page receives wakes over a stream" red: the spec's
premise (the dev server writes records constantly) is false once the page has loaded, and its first
assertion waits on the call resolving, which waits on a frame that a silent process never writes.

Two repairs, and the choice between them is the user's:

- Give the binary envelope a keepalive. A new frame flag (a frame with no value) that
  `valuesOfFrame` skips, written on the same idle timer the text envelope uses. It flushes the
  headers, so a reader sees the stream open immediately, and it makes quiet distinguishable from
  dead for every binary consumer — the CLI, an agent, a page. Touches
  `core/blong-mle/src/streamFrame.ts` (the flag), `core/blong-gogo/src/gatewayStream.ts` (write it,
  and stop tying the heartbeat to the text envelope), and the readers. A protocol addition, so it
  needs a decision of its own.
- Make the spec write the record it waits for. The premise becomes true rather than assumed: after
  the page opens, the test performs one served call (which writes records), then asserts a wake
  arrives and the stream is open. The product keeps a 15s silence on a quiet process, which is
  defensible for a log tail but leaves the page's own diagnostic weaker than it reads.

Until one is chosen the spec stays red, and the three fixes beneath it (the packet shape in
`loop.ts`, the same packet in the route's `_streamFrames`, and the ten-second http timeout a stream
inherited) stay verified by the tap suites and the framework's 1354 tests.

Done as D-955: the binary envelope carries a keepalive frame (STREAM_FLAG_KEEPALIVE, written at open
and on each idle tick, never sealed, skipped by valuesOfFrame), and writeEventStream no longer ties
the heartbeat to the text envelope. The portal's log page now reports its stream open immediately on
a quiet process, and the browser spec asserts the subscription outlives the five-second fallback
instead of waiting for a record a silent process never writes. Four tests cover it (writer, sealed
route, silent stream, reader), blong-gogo is 1365 with 0 failures, and both packages lint clean.

### T-754 — MLE seals an absent result as the text undefined

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · done_

In core/blong-gogo/src/mle.ts, preSerialization serialises where.result and where.error with
reply.serializeInput and seals whatever comes back. With the permissive schema a flow.find uses
(type.Unknown() compiles to an empty schema) fast-json-stringify renders an absent value as the four
characters undefined, so a handler that answers nothing ships a sealed envelope whose payload is not
JSON, and the browser reports a SyntaxError rather than the missing answer. The same defect exists
one layer down and is worth fixing there instead: a plain envelope is built as result: undefined,
JSON.stringify drops the key, and the client's jsonrpc receive refuses a body with no result at all
(jsonrpcEmpty) — so a handler that answers nothing has no valid answer in either shape, and MLE only
makes it unreadable. Answer null on the server (or a typed empty-answer error) for both shapes, with
a test per shape: a route declaring result: type.Unknown() and a handler returning undefined, once
plain and once sealed. Reproduce today with the blong-gateway realm: make a blong.* read answer
nothing and the observedFlow spec fails with the parse error.

Fixed: gatewayAnswer.jsonRpcAnswer builds the JSON-RPC body with the result coerced by `?? null`, so

### T-752 — A schema validation failure answers 500, not 400

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · done_

The gateway answers a failed schema validation with 500 and an unhandled-error record. In the
deployed suite the runbook's own negative call, POST /rpc/access/access/edit with isActive set to
not-a-boolean, is what a reader sees in the login pod as gateway unhandled error with a stack. The
call is deliberate: portalChecks sends a payload no model allows and only requires the body to say
must be boolean, so the run is green while the pod reports a failure that means nothing. The cause
is the validator compiler in core/blong-gogo/src/Gateway.ts: it returns a plain Error from
Value.Check, with no statusCode and no type, so the error handler falls back to 500 and logs at
error level. A bad request should come back as a typed 4xx validation error that the expected-errors
rules can recognise, which also makes the log quiet for a caller's mistake. Changing this changes a
client-visible status code for every suite, so it needs its own change with the framework tests that
pin gateway error shapes, and portalChecks should then assert the status rather than the text.

Fixed: the validator compiler returns a typed gateway.validationFailed (400) carrying validation as
the list of field-and-message pairs the browser's Editor paints, and the problems in its message;
gatewayValidation.ts holds the conversion with its own tests. portalChecks now judges the refusal by
status and type and declares it in expect, so the deployment's log stays quiet. blong-gogo 1392 with
0 failures; blong-int-kustomize 15/15.

### T-711 — Register the lukaot layer and route its declarations to the registry

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · done_

Planned in [#277](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/277).

Add `lukaot` to `WELL_KNOWN_LAYERS` in `core/blong-lib/layers.ts` with the `error` layer's
activation (`microservice`, `k8s`, `upgrade`), a row in the conventions layer table, and the kukum
primitive that scaffolds `lukaot/{error,signal}.ts`. Then find the seam that makes `error/error.ts`
reach `ErrorFactory.register`: its default export is a plain object, so `kind()` is empty and no
branch of `layerProxy`'s switch matches it — pin the current behaviour with a test first, then hand
both folders' declaration objects to the same registrar.

- verify: a framework test asserts a declaration in `lukaot/error.ts` and one in `lukaot/signal.ts`
  are both reachable from a handler's destructure, and that `error/error.ts` still registers.

Progress (2026-11-18): the layer is registered, the conventions table and the generated page carry
it, the kukum primitive scaffolds both declaration files, and the registrar now exists.

`declare()` sets the framework's kind symbol (`Symbol.for('blong:kind')`, non-enumerable) so a
declaration arrives as `object:vocabulary`; lukaot still imports nothing from blong. `layerProxy`
gained that case — the error half goes to `target.error` (the bound `ErrorFactory.register`) and the
whole declaration is pushed onto `result.vocabulary`, where the proxy will be built from it — and a
fallback case for a bare `object:` whose file is `error.ts`, which is what registers the legacy map.

That fallback is a behaviour change and it was worth making: `Errors.get(type)` returns a lazily
built default for an unregistered name, so every realm's `error/error.ts` has been silently ignored
— it threw with a generated message and no declared status. With the map registered, `blong-gogo`
(1241 assertions), `realm/blong-chat` (111) and `realm/blong-kustomize` (149) all still pass, so
nothing depended on the generated default.

What remains: the `signal` half. It needs a proxy a handler reaches as `this.signal`, built from the
vocabularies the loader collected and emitting through the port's log — and that runs into a bundle
question the next run must settle first: `layerProxy` and `Watch` are shared with the browser
loader, and lukaot's root reaches `node:async_hooks`, so the wiring has to be constructed where the
log is (the port's init, which is already server-side) rather than imported into the shared loader.
A unit test that drove `layerProxy` directly was attempted and abandoned — the closure it builds is
not invocable without the port — so the pin belongs at the loader level, in a fixture realm, which
is the same test the verify asks for.

lukaot is a well-known layer; declare() marks a declaration with the framework's kind symbol;
layerProxy registers a vocabulary's errors with ErrorFactory and keeps it on the layer result, and
registers a legacy error/error.ts map too (which had been silently dropped since the folder existed
— Errors.get builds a default for an unregistered name). signals.ts builds the flat vocabulary a
handler calls as this.signal from the layer's declarations, writing each record through the port's
own logger; the attacher is resolved lazily and never in the browser, so a process that declares
nothing loads nothing. blong-gogo 1255 assertions, blong-chat 111, kukum 669, blong-lib 224,
lukaot 21.

### T-712 — Load declared vocabularies and hand them to the runtime proxy

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · done_

Planned in [#277](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/277).

`src/lukaotVocabulary.ts` composes the declarations found in each realm's `lukaot` layer — and,
until a realm is converted, in its `error` layer — into one registry per realm, merges the realm's
`lukaot.policy` config, and hands `Registry._createHandlers` the `signal` and `errors` proxies. The
`lib` proxy gains `signal`; `errors` keeps the camelCase lookup, the `errorX` spelling unconverted
realms use, and the "available errors" message.

- verify: a framework test asserts a handler reaches `signal` and `errors` by destructuring, and
  that an undeclared method is absent rather than throwing.

Progress (2026-11-18): the composition and the proxy exist, under a different name and a narrower
scope than the plan expected, and the difference is worth stating before the rest is built.

`core/blong-gogo/src/signals.ts` (not `lukaotVocabulary.ts`) composes the declarations a layer
shipped into one registry and attaches the **flat** vocabulary to the port as `port.signal` — flat
because the plan's call sites are `this.signal?.agentTicketSkipped?.({...})`, and the full proxy,
with `reachable`/`sites`/`dependencies`, is returned to whoever asks the coverage questions. Each
record is written through the port's own logger at the level the policy resolved to, with the
identifier and the values as bindings, so a signal stays a log line where logs already go. An error
signal returns the failure to throw.

The scope is one **layer**, not one realm, and that is deliberate rather than a shortcut: a port
serves one namespace, a namespace is one layer's handlers, and a handler calling a name its own
layer did not declare is the mistake the vocabulary exists to catch. A realm that spreads its
declarations across `lukaot/error.ts` and `lukaot/signal.ts` still gets one registry, because both
files arrive through the same `lukaot` folder; what it does not get is a registry shared with a
_different_ layer of the same realm.

What is left for this task: merging the realm's `lukaot.policy` config into the registry (nothing
reads it yet, so a configured level or sample has no effect), the `lib.signal` half (a `library()`
function has no port), and the test at the loader level — a fixture realm whose handler destructures
`signal` and `errors` and whose undeclared method is absent. The seam those need is in place: the
declarations reach `attachSignals` with the port, and the config is on `layerApi.config`.

signals.ts composes a layer's declarations into one registry, merges the realm's lukaot.policy
(raising, sampling, switching off; an unmatched key warns through the port's log) and attaches the
flat vocabulary as port.signal, with the same object on lib so a library() function calls
lib.signal.x. The full proxy is returned for the coverage questions. signals.test.ts pins 21
assertions: a line at the declared level with the identifier bound, an error signal returning the
declared type and status, no signal for a layer that declared nothing, two vocabularies composing, a
repeated name refused, policy applied, and an undeclared identifier absent rather than throwing.
blong-gogo 1266 assertions.

### T-715 — Point the loader at lukaot and take pino out of the framework

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · done_

Planned in [#277](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/277).

- verify: `cd core/blong-gogo && blong-dev test` passes, and `grep -rF 'semantic-log'` and
  `grep -rF '"pino"'` over the package both find nothing. **Both hold** (2026-11-19): the package's
  suite is 1203 assertions, and neither name appears in its source or its `package.json`.

DONE (2026-11-19). `src/LukaotLog.ts` is the framework's `ILog` over lukaot: one function translates
the two calling conventions, `$meta` is _moved_ onto `messageId`/`operation` rather than copied (a
copy printed the envelope twice — on the header and again as a detail block), `fatal` maps to
`error` because lukaot's `fatal` exits the process by contract, and `child` answers a pino-shaped
face because two components hand it to fastify as `loggerInstance`. It opens lukaot's cache from the
`{dir, limit}` block and starts the cluster service lazily, publishing `clusterUrl` so a realm's
port learns where to read its flows — the half whose absence made `blong.flow.find` fail before. One
service per process, its listener `unref`fed: a service per log instance gave every reader a
different ledger and kept a test process alive past its last assertion.

Deleted with the two variants: `SemanticLog.ts`, `SemanticLog.test.ts`, `semanticRecord.ts`,
`Log.ts`, `pino-pretty.ts`/`.mjs`, `pino-cacache.ts`/`.mjs`, `pino-pretty.test.ts`. The tests worth
keeping were ported to the new implementation (`log.level.test.ts`, `log.progress.test.ts`), and the
ones whose subject no longer exists (`SemanticLog.test.ts`) went with it — the suite lost 78
assertions and gained the 19 in `LukaotLog.test.ts`.

The facade moved in the same step (@@D-905): `responseContext.ts`, `checkpoint.ts` and `Registry.ts`
read `@feasibleone/lukaot/context`, `Gateway.ts` reads `TRACE_HEADER`/`withoutCapabilities` from
lukaot, and `loadServer.ts` attaches lukaot's own root as the vocabulary — one `AsyncLocalStorage`,
so an identity bound where a call is made is the one the emitter reads.

`core/blong` stopped borrowing pino's types: `Level`, `LevelWithSilent`, `LogFn` and `IChildLogger`
are declared there. `LogFn` had to become `(...args: unknown[]) => void` rather than a typed
two-argument shape — the framework's own helpers ask for `(...args: unknown[]) => void`, and a
narrower signature is not assignable to it despite accepting everything in practice.
`IChildLogger`'s members are required, not optional, because fastify's `FastifyBaseLogger` requires
them and an optional `child` is not a `FastifyBaseLogger`.

Two things stayed, and are recorded rather than quietly dropped. `log.impl` is still accepted and
ignored, because every deployment in the tree names `semantic` and refusing it would break them for
a word that now means nothing. And `AdapterBase.error()` keeps its line: the original task removed
it on the grounds that an error records itself when it is constructed, which is true of a lukaot
_error signal_ and not of an `ITypedError` from the framework's own factory — removing it would have

emitter (@@D-905) and the de-logging of `AdapterBase.error()` was dropped with its reason (@@D-907).

### T-722 — Verify the framework's error and logging contract end to end

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · done_

Planned in [#277](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/277).

`src/contract.test.ts` holds the framework's error contract against the emitter that now writes it —
four promises, each of which a rewrite could quietly break. An expected error (`$meta.expect` names
it) is demoted to `debug`, and at `info` it is filtered exactly as it always was. An unexpected one
records at `error` with `type` and `statusCode` on the record, and with the message and stack in the
logger's error slot — the two things that were lost when the error was handed over as a
_bag of fields_: `Error`'s members are not enumerable, so the record had an empty message and no
stack at all (@@D-907). The caller gets back the very object it handed over, stamped with
`$meta.method`, so a caller can rethrow what was recorded. And a `silent` error writes no line and
retains nothing.

The method is exercised through `AdapterBase.prototype` rather than through a constructed adapter:
what is under test is `error()` and the log it writes through, and a full adapter would bring an
API, a registry and a queue to a question about one method. 14 assertions.

Building it found a real regression, and the fix is in the implementation rather than in the test.
Giving a level face only the members its threshold allowed looked tidier and broke the demotion:
`error()` asks a face bound at `info` for `debug`, found no such method, and wrote _nothing_ — so an
expected failure vanished instead of being filtered by the threshold. A level face now carries every
member and the logger decides, which is what the face promised before this implementation existed.
Three tests moved with it: the two that asserted the absent member, and the level test that read the
same shape.

Gates: `blong-gogo` 1230 assertions, lint clean.

Four promises asserted, 14 assertions; found and fixed a level-face regression where a demoted
expected error wrote nothing.
